title: Parsing & Grammars
summary: Turning a flat token stream into structure using context-free grammars — top-down recursive descent, precedence climbing, and the bottom-up intuition behind LR parsing.

slides.markdown:
[lexical-analysis](lexical-analysis) produces a flat sequence of tokens with no relationships between them. Parsing's job is to impose the structure a flat sequence can't express on its own: that `2 + 3 * 4` groups as `2 + (3 * 4)`, that a `return` belongs to the function containing it, that an `if`'s `else` attaches to a specific `if`.

That structure comes from a **context-free grammar** — a set of rules for what a valid sequence of tokens looks like — and a parser is an algorithm that checks a token stream against that grammar while simultaneously building a tree that captures the structure it found. Two families of algorithm do this: **top-down**, starting from the overall goal and working down to the tokens, and **bottom-up**, starting from the tokens and working up to the goal.

Most hand-written parsers you'll ever touch are top-down. Most parser-generator output is bottom-up. Knowing why is the point of this topic.

slides.subTitle: Productions, terminals, non-terminals
slides.markdown:
A grammar is a set of **production rules**, each rewriting one **non-terminal** (a placeholder for structure, like `Expr`) into a sequence of **terminals** (actual tokens, like `NUM` or `PLUS`) and/or other non-terminals:

```text
Expr   -> Expr PLUS Term | Term
Term   -> Term STAR NUM | NUM
```

A **derivation** is repeatedly applying rules starting from a designated start non-terminal until you're left with only terminals — that sequence of rule applications *is* the structure a parser is trying to reconstruct from the token stream, just run in reverse: instead of generating tokens from the grammar, a parser infers which rules could have generated the tokens it was actually given.

![Parse tree for 2 + 3 * 4 showing multiplication nested deeper than addition](assets/precedence-parse-tree.svg)

Every internal node is a grammar rule that got applied; every leaf is an actual token from the input. The shape of the tree — multiplication nested inside addition — is precedence made visible: the grammar in the previous slide was written specifically so that `Term` (multiplication) can only appear as an operand of `Expr` (addition), never the reverse, which forces this exact nesting for any input.

assets.alt: Parse tree for 2 + 3 * 4 showing multiplication nested deeper than addition

slides.markdown:
**Recursive descent** is the direct, hand-writable translation of a grammar into code: one function per non-terminal, where each function's body mirrors that non-terminal's production rules — call the function for `Term` from inside the function for `Expr`, check for the literal token `PLUS` directly, and so on. It starts at the grammar's start symbol and works its way down toward the actual tokens, consuming them as it recognizes what rule it's inside.

Its appeal is directness: the code reads like the grammar, error messages can be crafted exactly where a specific rule fails, and there's no generator tool or build step involved. Its one structural weakness is the topic's next slide.

slides.sectionTitle: Why left recursion breaks recursive descent
slides.markdown:
A grammar rule like `Expr -> Expr PLUS Term | Term` is **left-recursive**: the very first thing `Expr` can produce is another `Expr`. Translated directly into a recursive-descent function, `parse_expr()` would call `parse_expr()` as its first action, which calls itself again as *its* first action, forever — infinite recursion with zero tokens ever consumed, and a stack overflow before any real parsing happens.

The fix is mechanical: rewrite left recursion into a loop. Instead of `Expr -> Expr PLUS Term | Term`, parse one `Term`, then **loop** consuming `PLUS Term` pairs for as long as they appear — the recursion becomes iteration, and the grammar's meaning is preserved because both formulations accept the identical language, just structured differently for the parsing algorithm's sake. This rewrite is routine enough that grammar textbooks give it a name (eliminating left recursion) and a mechanical procedure for the general case.

slides.subTitle: A practical favorite
slides.markdown:
Writing one grammar rule (and one parser function) per precedence level — `Expr`, `Term`, `Factor`, and so on for every operator tier — works but gets verbose fast once a language has many operators at many precedence levels (comparisons, boolean logic, bitwise ops, all with different binding strengths).

**Precedence climbing** (a form of Pratt parsing) collapses that into one loop: assign each operator a numeric precedence, parse one operand, then repeatedly check the next operator's precedence against a running threshold, recursing only when a *higher*-precedence operator needs to bind tighter first. This is genuinely how many production parsers handle expressions — one function handling every precedence level via a small table, instead of one hand-nested function per level — and it's the standard practical answer when an interviewer asks you to extend a basic recursive-descent parser to handle more operators cleanly.

Bottom-up parsers work in the opposite direction from recursive descent: instead of starting at the grammar's goal and predicting what comes next, they start at the tokens and repeatedly recognize completed pieces of structure, building upward toward the goal.

The core operation is **shift-reduce**: **shift** a token from the input onto a stack; **reduce** the top of the stack when it matches the right-hand side of some grammar rule, replacing those symbols with the rule's left-hand non-terminal. Parsing `2 + 3`: shift `2`, reduce it to `Term` (matches a rule), shift `+`, shift `3`, reduce `3` to `Term`, then reduce `Term PLUS Term` to `Expr` once the whole right-hand side is on the stack. **LR parsers** (the family behind `yacc`/`bison`) are shift-reduce parsers with a table telling them exactly when to shift versus reduce for any grammar in the class they support.

```python
# grammar: expr -> term (('+'|'-') term)*
#          term -> NUM (('*'|'/') NUM)*
def parse_expr(tokens):
    left = parse_term(tokens)
    while tokens.peek() in ('+', '-'):
        op = tokens.next()
        right = parse_term(tokens)
        left = BinOp(op, left, right)
    return left

def parse_term(tokens):
    left = tokens.next()          # expects NUM
    while tokens.peek() in ('*', '/'):
        op = tokens.next()
        right = tokens.next()      # expects NUM
        left = BinOp(op, left, right)
    return left
```

Notice the left-recursion fix from earlier already applied: `parse_expr` doesn't call itself first — it parses one `term`, then loops. Precedence falls straight out of the *call* structure: `parse_expr` calls `parse_term`, so multiplication always finishes binding before addition gets a chance to, with zero explicit precedence numbers anywhere in this version.

`if (a) if (b) x(); else y();` is genuinely **ambiguous** by the naive grammar `Stmt -> IF Expr Stmt | IF Expr Stmt ELSE Stmt` — the `else` could attach to the inner `if (b)` or the outer `if (a)`, and both are valid parses of the identical token sequence under that grammar.

Every mainstream language resolves this the same way: **attach the else to the nearest unmatched if** — a convention, not something inherent to the grammar. Parser generators handle it either by rewriting the grammar to make the nearest-if binding the *only* valid derivation (adding a non-terminal that explicitly distinguishes "statement with a matched else" from "statement that might still need one"), or by an explicit precedence/associativity directive telling the tool which shift-reduce choice to prefer when the ambiguity shows up in the parsing table. Either way, the fix is deliberate — an ambiguous grammar left unresolved would make the language's own behavior implementation-defined, which no real language ships with.

slides.sectionTitle: A grammar that looks right but isn't
slides.markdown:
Two failure modes hide in grammars that look perfectly reasonable on paper: genuine **ambiguity** (more than one valid parse tree for some input — dangling-else is the classic case) and **unbounded lookahead** (a parser needing to see arbitrarily far ahead in the token stream before it can decide which rule applies, which most practical parsing techniques can't do efficiently).

Both are easy to miss by eyeballing a grammar and hard to catch without either formal tooling (a parser generator will often report a shift-reduce or reduce-reduce conflict) or testing it against genuinely tricky inputs, not just the happy-path examples that motivated writing the rule in the first place. A grammar that parses every example you tried while writing it is not the same claim as a grammar that's unambiguous — the two properties are unrelated, and only one of them can be checked by example-based testing.

| | Hand-written recursive descent | Parser generator (yacc/ANTLR) |
|---|---|---|
| Control over error messages | Full — craft exactly where you want | Limited to what the tool exposes |
| Handles ambiguity | You resolve it explicitly in code | Tool reports conflicts, you adjust the grammar |
| Dev speed for a new grammar | Slower — write every function by hand | Fast — grammar file in, parser out |
| Debuggability | Straightforward — it's just a call stack | Harder — errors reference generated table states |

Production compilers for major languages disproportionately hand-write their parsers (Clang, `rustc`, Go's compiler) specifically for the error-message control — a compiler's parser errors are one of the most user-visible parts of the whole toolchain. Generators earn their keep for grammars that change often, or where dev speed matters more than message polish, like DSLs and internal tools.

slides.sectionTitle: Extending a parser with parens and precedence
slides.markdown:
"Extend this expression parser to support parentheses and precedence" is really testing whether you understand that the call structure of recursive descent *is* precedence — the fix is almost always small once that's clear.

Parentheses: add a rule at the *highest*-precedence level (typically inside whatever function handles the tightest-binding operands, like `parse_factor`) that checks for `(`, recursively calls all the way back to `parse_expr` to parse whatever's inside, then consumes the matching `)`. This works because a parenthesized expression can contain anything, including lower-precedence operators, so it has to re-enter parsing from the top, not from wherever the current call happens to be.

Adding a new precedence level (say, exponentiation binding tighter than multiplication): insert one more function between the existing two in the call chain, with the new operator's parsing logic, and rewire the adjacent functions' calls to route through it. Each new precedence level is one more rung in the call-stack ladder — the mechanical nature of this extension is exactly why interviewers use it as a follow-up.

A parser's output is a tree that captures every grammar rule applied and every token consumed — but that tree is usually noisier than it needs to be, carrying grammar-level scaffolding (intermediate non-terminals that exist only to make precedence work, punctuation tokens that don't affect meaning) that the next stage doesn't want to deal with.

[asts-and-semantic-analysis](asts-and-semantic-analysis) covers exactly that next step: collapsing the raw parse tree into a cleaner **AST** that keeps only what matters for checking meaning, and then checking that meaning — scope, types — against a program that's now known to be *structurally* valid but not yet known to make any sense.
